Western States Reclamation Bureau As-Built Construction Report — Juniper Canyon Dam
1.0 PROJECT DESCRIPTION
Juniper Canyon Dam is a 185-foot-high concrete gravity dam with earthen embankment abutment transitions,
located on the East Fork of the Juniper River in Owyhee County, Idaho, approximately 35 miles south of
Grandview. The dam was authorized by the Reclamation Project Act of 1956 and designed by the Western
States Reclamation Bureau (WSRB), Boise Regional Office, between 1958-1960. Construction was performed
by Morrison-Pacific Constructors, Inc. under Contract No. JC-1182-C between March 1960 - September 1963. This report documents the as-built conditions of the completed dam as of October 1963, when first filling
commenced. The dam impounds Juniper Canyon Reservoir, a 32,000-acre-foot irrigation storage reservoir extending 4.2
miles upstream. The reservoir provides irrigation water to approximately 48,000 acres of farmland in the Juniper
Basin via the existing canal system, flood control for the lower East Fork valley, and 4.8 MW of hydroelectric
generation through two 2.4 MW Francis turbine units at the powerhouse located at the downstream toe of the
gravity section. Table 1-1: Dam and Reservoir Summary

Both embankments are symmetrically zoned with the impervious core (Zone 1) flanked by filter/drain zones
(Zone 2) and compacted rockfill shells (Zone 3). The core zone material was borrowed from a designated area
on the left canyon rim where residual soil and weathered tuff are present to a depth of 8 to 15 feet. This borrow
material classifies as CL-ML (silty clay to clayey silt) with liquid limits of 34 to 38, plasticity indices of 12 to 16,
and a clay fraction of 24 to 30 percent. The specific gravity of the core material is 2.67 to 2.69. 4.2 Core Compaction Control
Embankment construction was performed between June 1961 and July 1963. A total of 2,486 field density tests
were performed using the sand cone method (ASTM D1556). The core zone achieved an average relative
compaction of 95.4 percent of Standard Proctor maximum dry density (MDD = 108.2 pcf at OMC = 17.5
percent), with no test falling below the specified minimum of 93 percent. The placement moisture content
averaged 18.3 percent (OMC + 0.8%), with a range of 16.0 to 19.5 percent (OMC - 1.5% to OMC + 2.0%). The
slight wet-of-optimum average is desirable for a dam core, as it promotes higher saturation and lower
permeability in the as-placed condition. The standard Proctor compaction test (ASTM D698) was performed on composite samples from each day's
placement.

The standard Proctor compaction test (ASTM D698) was performed on composite samples from each day's
placement. The maximum dry density ranged from 107.5 to 109.2 pcf (mean 108.2 pcf), reflecting the moderate
variability in gradation of the borrow material. The permeability of the compacted core, measured on
undisturbed samples taken from test pits in the completed fill, averaged 5e-07 cm/s, which is within the range
expected for a well-compacted CL-ML fill and confirms that the core will function as an effective seepage
barrier. 4.3 Foundation Contact Treatment
The embankment foundation contact was prepared by stripping all overburden (alluvium, colluvium, residual
soil) to expose competent welded tuff or basalt. The exposed rock surface was cleaned by air-water jetting and
hand scaling. Dental concrete (3,000 psi) was placed to fill overhangs, depressions, and open joints at the
foundation contact. The core zone was placed directly on the prepared rock surface, with special attention to
compaction of the first lift against irregular rock contours. A grout cap (12-inch thick concrete slab) was placed
at the upstream edge of the core zone to seal the core-to-rock contact and provide the grout curtain platform. 5.0 FOUNDATION TREATMENT

Western States Reclamation Bureau As-Built Construction Report — Juniper Canyon Dam
The valley floor alluvium was stripped to competent welded tuff across the full 340-foot length of the gravity
section footprint. Maximum stripping depth was 15 feet at the center of the valley (Monolith 8). The exposed
rock surface was cleaned by air-water jetting at 150 psi, and all loose or weathered material was removed by
hand scaling. Dental concrete (3,000 psi) was placed in overhangs, seams, potholes, and irregularities to
provide a uniform contact surface. A total of 680 cubic yards of dental concrete was placed across the gravity
section and embankment foundations. On the canyon walls, the colluvium and residual soil were stripped to expose competent rock for the
embankment foundation contacts. On the right abutment, the basalt interbed provided an excellent bearing
surface at shallow depth. On the left abutment, partially welded tuff was encountered at the surface and was
excavated to a maximum depth of 18 feet before competent densely welded tuff was reached. This additional
excavation required a design modification to increase the left embankment shell volume by approximately 8,000
cubic yards. 5.2 Grout Curtain
A single-line grout curtain was constructed along the upstream face of the gravity section and continuing
through both embankment abutments, for a total curtain length of 620 feet. The curtain extends to 60 feet below
the foundation contact in the gravity section and 40 feet below the foundation contact in the embankments. Grout holes were drilled at 10-foot primary spacing, with split-spacing to 5 feet where refusal pressures
indicated additional treatment was needed. A total of 6,840 linear feet of grout holes were drilled and 18,200 sacks (94 lb each) of Type I Portland cement
were injected. The grout was mixed at water-to-cement ratios ranging from 5:1 (thin starting mix) to 0.6:1 (thick
final mix), following the standard WSRB split-spacing and thickening procedure. Grout pressures were limited to
0.5 psi per foot of overburden depth to prevent hydraulic fracturing of the foundation rock. The shear zone required special treatment.

Grout pressures were limited to
0.5 psi per foot of overburden depth to prevent hydraulic fracturing of the foundation rock. The shear zone required special treatment. Within the 40-foot zone where the shear zone crosses the grout
curtain alignment (approximately Station 7+60 to 8+00), grout consumption was extraordinarily high — 3,200
sacks of cement were injected in this 40-foot zone alone, representing 18 percent of the total grout consumption
for the entire dam. The clay gouge and fractured rock surrounding the shear zone accepted large volumes of
thin grout (5:1 to 3:1 w:c), indicating highly permeable conditions prior to treatment. Multiple stages of re-drilling
and re-grouting were required before acceptable refusal pressures were achieved. Post-grouting water
pressure tests confirmed that the curtain reduced the shear zone permeability from approximately 35 Lugeon to
3 Lugeon (a 92 percent reduction), meeting the design criterion of less than 5 Lugeon. WSRB Project No. JC-1182 Page 7

Western States Reclamation Bureau As-Built Construction Report — Juniper Canyon Dam
5.3 Foundation Drains
A total of 42 foundation drain holes were drilled vertically from the drainage gallery floor at 10-foot spacing
along the full length of the gallery. Each drain is 3 inches in diameter and extends 40 feet below the gallery
floor, inclined 15 degrees downstream to intercept seepage that passes through or around the grout curtain. The drains are uncased open holes in competent rock, with 3-inch PVC standpipes and flow measurement
weirs at the gallery floor. The drain system is designed to reduce uplift pressure at the gallery floor from the full headwater pressure
(without drains) to 33 percent of headwater pressure (with functional drains), per the WSRB gravity dam design
standard. This uplift reduction is the primary mechanism for maintaining adequate sliding stability. The 66
percent drain efficiency threshold established by FHSC guidelines represents the minimum performance
required to maintain the design factor of safety against sliding. During initial operation (first filling, October 1963 to June 1964), the drains performed excellently. Individual
drain flows ranged from 0.8 to 5.2 gpm, with total gallery drain flow of 120 gpm at normal pool.

content:
8.0 INITIAL OBSERVATIONS AND FIRST FILLING
First filling commenced on October 12, 1963 when the river diversion outlets were closed. The reservoir rose
steadily through the winter and spring, reaching normal pool (El. 5195.0) on June 8, 1964, and maximum pool
(El. 5200.0) on June 22, 1964 during spring snowmelt. The total filling period was approximately 8 months. The
maximum rate of reservoir rise was 1.2 feet per day during the May-June snowmelt period. 8.1 Seepage Observations
Seepage was first detected at the left abutment toe at a reservoir elevation of approximately El. 5,090 (March
1964, approximately 73 feet of head). At full pool, the seepage measurements were as follows: left abutment 8
gpm, right abutment 5 gpm, gallery drains 120 gpm, for a total of 133 gpm. The seepage was clear at all
locations with no turbidity, discoloration, or suspended material, indicating no internal erosion or material
transport. The seepage response was linear with reservoir level — each foot of head increase produced a
proportional increase in seepage flow — confirming Darcy-type laminar flow through the rock mass rather than
concentrated piping channels. The left abutment seepage (8 gpm) was consistently higher than the right abutment (5 gpm) at all pool levels,
which is attributed to residual seepage along the shear zone beneath the left portion of the gravity section and
left abutment. This was anticipated in the design, and the measured seepage rate is within the range predicted
by the pre-construction seepage analysis (6-12 gpm at normal pool). 8.2 Uplift and Drain Performance

title: AS-BUILT CONSTRUCTION REPORT
content:
9.0 CONCLUSIONS
Juniper Canyon Dam was constructed in accordance with the WSRB design specifications and contract
requirements. All quality control testing met or exceeded the specified criteria. The first filling period
demonstrated satisfactory performance of all dam components:
The concrete gravity section achieved a mean 28-day compressive strength of 5,180 psi, exceeding the 4,500
psi design minimum. The grout curtain reduced foundation permeability to less than 5 Lugeon throughout its
length, including the challenging shear zone section where 3,200 sacks of grout were required. The foundation
drain system achieved 85 percent efficiency, exceeding the 80 percent target, and reduced uplift to 28 percent
of headwater (below the 33 percent design assumption). Seepage at first filling totaled 133 gpm and was clear at all locations. Structural deflections were within 10
percent of design predictions. The WSRB Materials Laboratory noted the potentially reactive aggregate and
recommended monitoring for alkali-silica reaction during the service life of the structure. No other concerns
were identified. The dam is cleared for normal operation under the terms of FHSC License No. 5847. WSRB Project No. JC-1182 Page 11

title: AS-BUILT CONSTRUCTION REPORT
content:
Western States Reclamation Bureau As-Built Construction Report — Juniper Canyon Dam
The Juniper Canyon dam site is located in the Owyhee volcanic field, a thick sequence of Miocene volcanic
rocks overlain by thin Quaternary alluvial and colluvial deposits. Six exploratory borings (BH-1 through BH-6)
were drilled during the design investigation in 1958-1959. The subsurface conditions are described below from
top to bottom. 2.1 Overburden
Valley floor alluvium consists of dense, well-graded gravel and sand with cobbles (USCS classification
GP-GW), ranging from 0 to 15 feet thick at the dam axis. The alluvium is highly pervious and was entirely
stripped during foundation preparation. Canyon wall colluvium, ranging from 5 to 20 feet thick, consists of
angular tuff fragments in a silt and gravel matrix (GM-GC). Residual soil on the canyon rims is a thin (0 to 5
feet) sandy silt (ML) formed by weathering of the underlying tuff. All overburden was removed from the dam
footprint and embankment foundation contact areas. 2.2 Bedrock — Rhyolite Welded Tuff
The primary foundation rock is the Salmon Creek Tuff, a Miocene-age rhyolite ignimbrite (welded tuff) with
eutaxitic texture — flattened pumice fiamme in a matrix of welded glass shards and crystal fragments. The tuff
exhibits a welding gradient that strongly influences its engineering properties. Densely welded zones are
salmon-pink to gray, hard, competent, and have unconfined compressive strengths of 12,200 to 17,800 psi
based on testing of cores from the design-phase borings. Rock Quality Designation (RQD) in the densely
welded zones averages 82 percent, indicating good to excellent rock mass quality. Unit weight of the densely
welded tuff is 152 pcf. Partially welded to non-welded zones occur at the top and base of the ignimbrite cooling unit and are
significantly weaker, with UCS of 1,500 to 3,800 psi and RQD of 15 to 35 percent. These zones are porous,
permeable, and weather readily along joint surfaces.

title: AS-BUILT CONSTRUCTION REPORT
content:
These zones are porous,
permeable, and weather readily along joint surfaces. Where partially welded tuff was encountered at the
foundation contact (primarily on the canyon rims at the left and right abutments), it was either excavated to
competent densely welded tuff or treated with dental concrete and consolidation grouting. The rhyolite tuff contains devitrified volcanic glass — the original volcanic glass has partially crystallized to
microcrystalline silica (cristobalite and tridymite). Petrographic examination of the coarse aggregate source
material (the same welded tuff, from the on-site quarry) identified this devitrified glass as a potentially
alkali-reactive constituent. Mortar bar testing per ASTM C227 (1-year duration) yielded an expansion of 0.08
percent, which was below the 0.10 percent expansion threshold used at the time of design (1959). However,
the cement alkali content of 0.68 percent NanO equivalent exceeds the limit of 0.60 percent that would later be
adopted by ACI 201 for use with potentially reactive aggregates. No supplementary cementitious material
(pozzolan or fly ash) was specified in the original mix design to mitigate potential alkali-silica reactivity. 2.3 Bedrock — Basalt Interbeds
Olivine basalt flows of Miocene age are interbedded with the welded tuff sequence and were encountered in
borings BH-3, BH-5, and BH-6. The basalt is dense, dark gray to black, massive, and very hard, with UCS of
26,500 to 34,200 psi and RQD of 85 to 98 percent. Unit weight is 172 pcf. The basalt interbeds are excellent
foundation rock where encountered; however, the flow contacts (upper and lower surfaces of each flow) are
vesicular and highly permeable, with Lugeon values of 15 to 35 prior to grouting. These permeable contacts
required careful attention during grout curtain construction. 2.4 Bedrock — Tuffaceous Interbeds
Thin (1 to 3 feet) interbeds of tuffaceous sandstone and siltstone occur between the major tuff units.

2.4 Bedrock — Tuffaceous Interbeds
Thin (1 to 3 feet) interbeds of tuffaceous sandstone and siltstone occur between the major tuff units. These
interbeds are weak (UCS 600 to 1,800 psi), erodible, and have low RQD (15 to 25 percent). Where

encountered at shallow depth on the canyon rims, these interbeds were excavated. At depth, they do not
control foundation stability because they are thin, discontinuous, and bounded by competent welded tuff above
and below. 2.5 Shear Zone
A prominent shear zone was identified in BH-3 at 42 feet depth and confirmed in BH-4 at 28 feet depth, allowing
its geometry to be established: 2-4 feet wide, dipping approximately 35 degrees downstream (southeast). The
zone consists of intensely sheared and crushed rock with a central gouge seam of high-plasticity clay (USCS
classification CH, liquid limit 52, plasticity index 28). The gouge surfaces are slickensided, indicating previous
shear displacement along this feature. The shear zone crosses the gravity section foundation beneath approximately Monoliths 6 through 9 at depths
of 35 to 55 feet below the foundation contact, depending on canyon location. It intersects the left abutment
embankment foundation at approximately 65 to 72 feet depth. The zone was treated by extensive consolidation
and curtain grouting during construction (see Section 5.2). Post-construction Lugeon testing confirmed that the
grouting reduced the shear zone permeability from approximately 35 Lugeon to less than 5 Lugeon, and the
foundation drain system was designed to intercept any residual seepage along this feature. WSRB Project No.

The concrete mix was designed by the WSRB Materials Laboratory in Denver. Type II cement was selected for
moderate sulfate resistance, as the groundwater in the tuffaceous foundation rock has sulfate concentrations of
200 to 500 ppm. The cement was supplied by the Idaho Portland Cement Company, Inkom, Idaho, in bulk by
rail to the Grandview siding and trucked to the site. 3.2 Aggregate Source and Processing
Coarse aggregate was produced from an on-site quarry in the densely welded tuff on the right abutment rim,
approximately 1,200 feet downstream of the dam axis. The tuff was drilled, blasted, and processed through a
three-stage crushing plant (jaw, cone, and impact crushers) to produce crushed material with a maximum size
of 3 inches. The aggregate is hard, angular, and well-graded, with Los Angeles abrasion loss of 22 percent
(within the 40 percent limit). Specific gravity is 2.42 and absorption is 1.8 percent (higher than typical for
concrete aggregate due to the vesicular texture of the tuff). As noted in Section 2.2, petrographic examination identified devitrified volcanic glass in the aggregate as a
potentially alkali-reactive constituent.

title: AS-BUILT CONSTRUCTION REPORT
content:
As noted in Section 2.2, petrographic examination identified devitrified volcanic glass in the aggregate as a
potentially alkali-reactive constituent. The ASTM C227 mortar bar test yielded 0.08 percent expansion at 1 year,
below the 0.10 percent threshold of the 1958 ASTM standard. The WSRB Materials Laboratory noted this result
in their aggregate qualification report (WSRB Lab Report AG-1182-03, March 1959) and recommended
monitoring for alkali-silica reaction during the service life of the structure. However, no pozzolan or low-alkali
cement was specified because the test result was below the applicable threshold, and the use of supplementary
cementitious materials for ASR mitigation was not yet standard practice in 1959. The cement alkali content of
0.68 percent NanO equivalent was not identified as a concern at the time of design. Fine aggregate was produced from alluvial deposits in the East Fork Juniper River channel, approximately 2
miles upstream of the dam site. The alluvial sand is predominantly quartz and feldspar with minor lithic
fragments, well-graded (fineness modulus 2.75), and met all ASTM C33 gradation requirements. Specific
gravity is 2.62 and absorption is 0.9 percent. 3.3 Concrete Placement

title: AS-BUILT CONSTRUCTION REPORT
content:
Western States Reclamation Bureau As-Built Construction Report — Juniper Canyon Dam
Mass concrete placement commenced on April 12, 1961 and was completed on September 28, 1963, a total
placement period of 30 months. The total volume of structural concrete placed in the gravity section was
128,500 cubic yards, including the spillway ogee crest, stilling basin, gallery, and foundation contact zone. Concrete was placed in 5-foot horizontal lifts to control thermal gradients during hydration. Each monolith was
placed independently, with contraction joints between monoliths sealed with copper waterstops and filled with a
compressible filler. Peak placement rates reached 850 cubic yards per day during the summer months (June through September)
when ambient temperatures permitted round-the-clock placement. Winter placement (November through
March) was suspended when sustained ambient temperatures fell below 35°F, per WSRB specification. Hot-weather placement above 90°F required the use of chilled mixing water and ice to maintain concrete
placement temperature below 70°F. Curing was by water ponding on horizontal surfaces and burlap/curing
compound on vertical forms. A total of 342 test cylinders were cast during placement (one set of three per 100 cubic yards). The 28-day
compressive strength averaged 5,180 psi with a range of 4,340 to 6,020 psi. Only one cylinder (4,340 psi) fell
below the specified minimum of 4,500 psi, giving a pass rate of 99.7 percent. The air content averaged 5.2
percent with a pass rate of 96.5 percent (range 3.8 to 6.5 percent). Strength gain over time was consistent with
Type II cement hydration — 90-day strengths averaged 6,420 psi and 1-year strengths averaged 6,980 psi from
retained test specimens. WSRB Project No. JC-1182 Page 5

State Division of Water Resources 30-Year Dam Safety Inspection — Juniper Canyon Dam
1.0 INSPECTION SUMMARY
The State Division of Water Resources (SDWR) conducted a comprehensive dam safety inspection of Juniper
Canyon Dam on September 15-16, 1995, in coordination with the Juniper Basin Irrigation District operations
staff. The inspection was performed at the 30-year mark following first filling (1964). The dam was inspected
under normal pool conditions (El. 5195 ft). 2.0 CONDITION OBSERVATIONS
2.1 Concrete Gravity Section
The downstream face is in generally good condition. No structural cracking or displacement was observed. Minor surface scaling (less than 0.25 inches depth) was noted on the upstream face between El. 5,168 and El. 5,182, in the zone of normal water surface fluctuation. This scaling is attributed to freeze-thaw action and is
considered cosmetic at this stage. No alkali-silica reaction (ASR) indicators were observed during this
inspection; however, the early stage of ASR may not be visually apparent. The drainage gallery is dry and accessible. All 42 foundation drains are flowing. Several drains (Drains 18, 19,
and 21) show visible calcium carbonate deposits (white mineral buildup) around the drain collars, indicating the
beginning of drain clogging. No drains were fully plugged at the time of inspection. 2.2 Embankments
Both embankment abutments are in good condition. No slumping, settlement, cracking, or animal burrows were
observed on the slopes. Vegetation (native grasses) is established on both downstream slopes. Seepage
collection ditches are clear and flowing. No wet areas, boils, or turbidity in seepage. 2.3 Spillway and Gates
All three radial gates were operated during the inspection. Gates 1 and 3 operated normally. Gate 2 required
additional hydraulic pressure to initiate movement and showed visible surface corrosion on the downstream
skin plate.

generation. The dam is classified as High Hazard (Category I) under FHSC guidelines, with an estimated
downstream population at risk of approximately 2,400 persons in the Grandview area, 32 miles downstream. The inspection team consisted of R. A. Caldwell, P.E. (CDSC Principal Engineer and Independent Consultant,

Inspector). The three-day inspection included visual examination of all dam components, review of

records.

3.5 Issue 5 — Seismic Re-evaluation Required (MODERATE Priority)
The National Geophysical Survey Institute (NGSI) published an updated National Seismic Hazard Model in
2018 that significantly increased the design ground motions applicable to the Juniper Canyon Dam site. The
Peak Ground Acceleration (PGA) for the 2,475-year return period (the standard design earthquake for dam
safety evaluations) increased from the value used in the original 1958 design (0.10g, based on pseudo-static
analysis) to 0.18g — an 80 percent increase. The Maximum Credible Earthquake (MCE) PGA for the site is
now estimated at 0.22g. The increase is driven by updated characterization of the Owyhee Range Front Fault, located approximately 18
km from the dam site, which is now assessed as capable of generating a magnitude 7.0 earthquake with a
recurrence interval of 5,000 to 15,000 years. The Bruneau-Jarbidge Fault (35 km distant, M 6.5 capable) also
contributes to the site hazard. The original 1958 design used a pseudo-static coefficient of 0.10g, which was
standard practice at the time but does not meet current FHSC Engineering Guidelines Chapter 13 requirements
for seismic evaluation of concrete gravity dams. Consequence: The gravity section and both embankments were designed for seismic loading of 0.10g. Under
the updated hazard of 0.18g, the seismic demand is 80 percent higher than the original design basis. A formal
seismic re-evaluation is required per FHSC Engineering Guidelines, including updated stability analysis for the
gravity section (sliding, overturning), pseudo-static and Newmark displacement analysis for the embankments,
and assessment of concrete cracking potential under dynamic loading.

6.0 RECOMMENDATIONS
CDSC recommends that JBID initiate a comprehensive Periodic Safety Review (PSR) investigation to
address all five issues identified in this inspection. The PSR should include the following scope:
6.1 Geotechnical Drilling Program
Five exploratory borings are recommended: three in or adjacent to the gravity section (BH-GS-01 through
BH-GS-03) to characterize concrete condition, foundation rock properties, and shear zone behavior; and two
through the embankments (BH-LE-01 and BH-RE-01, one per abutment) to characterize embankment fill
properties and investigate the left abutment seepage path. BH-GS-01 should be drilled from the gallery floor
through the full dam section and into the foundation to obtain concrete cores at multiple depths and foundation
rock samples including the shear zone. Supplemental piezometers and an inclinometer should be installed in
the left embankment boring. 6.2 Laboratory Testing
Concrete core testing: compressive and splitting tensile strength at 4 to 6 depth intervals to quantify the
ASR/F-T damage gradient, petrographic analysis per ASTM C856 on at least 6 thin sections. Foundation rock
testing: UCS and ITS on welded tuff and basalt specimens, residual strength testing on shear zone clay gouge
(ring shear per ASTM D6467). Embankment testing: Atterberg limits, gradation with hydrometer, specific
gravity, moisture-density relationships, CU triaxial shear strength, falling-head permeability. 6.3 Foundation Drain Evaluation

3.1 Issue 1 — Foundation Drain Deterioration (HIGH Priority)
The foundation drain system is the single most critical safety feature of the gravity section, because it controls
the uplift pressure distribution beneath the dam. The original design assumed that the 42 foundation drains
would reduce uplift pressure at the gallery floor to 33 percent of headwater pressure, which is the basis for the
gravity section sliding stability calculation. When drain efficiency declines, uplift increases, and the factor of
safety against sliding decreases proportionally. Drain efficiency has declined steadily over the life of the dam. At first filling in 1964, drain efficiency was 85
percent — exceeding the 80 percent design target. By the 1995 dam safety inspection, efficiency had declined
to 72 percent but was still above the 66 percent FHSC guideline minimum. The decline has accelerated in
recent years: efficiency dropped from 65 percent in 2005 to 56 percent at the time of this inspection (2022),
falling below the 66 percent minimum for the first time in the dam's history. Table 3-1: Foundation Drain Performance History

title: PART 12D SAFETY INSPECTION REPORT
content:
At the time of inspection, CDSC counted 6 drains
with no visible flow (presumed fully clogged) and 14 drains with significantly reduced flow compared to historical
records. The remaining 22 drains appear functional, but even these show mineral coating on the bore walls. The clogging mechanism is well understood: seepage water dissolves calcium from the grout curtain cement
and the tuffaceous foundation rock; as the water enters the low-pressure drain environment, dissolved COn
degasses and calcium carbonate precipitates on the drain walls, progressively reducing the drain bore
diameter. Consequence: The declining drain efficiency has increased uplift pressure from the design value of 33 percent
to an estimated 44 percent of headwater pressure in 2022 (based on the gallery floor piezometer readings). This 11 percentage point increase in uplift translates directly to a reduction in the net downward force resisting
sliding. A formal stability re-evaluation is urgently needed to determine whether the current factor of safety
meets FHSC minimum criteria. If the drain efficiency continues to decline at the current rate (approximately 2
percentage points per 5 years), the drains will become completely non-functional within 25 to 30 years, at which
point the uplift pressure would reach approximately 67 percent of headwater — nearly double the design
assumption. 3.2 Issue 2 — Concrete Deterioration (HIGH Priority)
CDSC Project No. 2022-0215 Page 2

title: PART 12D SAFETY INSPECTION REPORT
content:
Cascade Dam Safety Consultants Part 12D Inspection — Juniper Canyon Dam
The gravity section concrete exhibits two distinct deterioration mechanisms that are acting synergistically to
degrade the upstream face of the dam. Both mechanisms have progressed significantly since the 2017 Part
12D inspection. 3.2.1 Freeze-Thaw Damage
The upstream face shows progressive freeze-thaw (F/T) damage between El. 5168 and El. 5182,
encompassing the 14-foot-high normal pool fluctuation zone where the concrete is subjected to repeated cycles
of wetting and freezing. This zone experiences the most severe exposure conditions: the concrete is saturated
by reservoir water during high pool, then exposed to sub-freezing temperatures (often -10°F to -20°F) during
winter drawdown at this 5,200-foot elevation. The site experiences an estimated 150 or more freeze-thaw
cycles per year. The damage has progressed significantly since the 2017 inspection. Surface scaling now extends to 1 to 2
inches depth over approximately 60 percent of the fluctuation zone area, compared to approximately 30 percent
in 2017. Several areas on Monoliths 6 through 9 (the tallest section) show deeper spalling to 3 to 4 inches, with
exposed coarse aggregate visible. The damage is most severe at Monolith 8 (the maximum height section,
where hydraulic head and saturation depth are greatest). The 1995 dam safety inspection documented only
minor scaling to 0.25-inch depth in this zone — the damage has increased by an order of magnitude in the
subsequent 27 years, suggesting an accelerating deterioration rate. 3.2.2 Alkali-Silica Reaction (ASR)
Alkali-silica reaction (ASR) has been positively identified on the downstream face of the gravity section. Map
cracking and white gel deposits were observed at multiple locations on Monoliths 6 through 10, concentrated in
the central (tallest) portion of the dam. The cracking pattern is characteristic of ASR: randomly oriented cracks
forming polygon shapes with 6 to 12-inch spacing, with white alkali-silica gel exuding from crack intersections. The gel is soft and moist, indicating that the reaction is still active. The original concrete used crushed rhyolite welded tuff (from the on-site quarry) as coarse aggregate.

title: PART 12D SAFETY INSPECTION REPORT
content:
The gel is soft and moist, indicating that the reaction is still active. The original concrete used crushed rhyolite welded tuff (from the on-site quarry) as coarse aggregate. This
material contains devitrified volcanic glass — a known alkali-reactive constituent. The WSRB Materials
Laboratory identified this reactivity during the design phase (WSRB Lab Report AG-1182-03, March 1959), but
the ASTM C227 mortar bar expansion of 0.08 percent was below the 0.10 percent threshold used at that time. The cement alkali content of 0.68 percent NanO equivalent was not considered problematic in 1959, but it
exceeds the 0.60 percent limit that was subsequently adopted by ACI 201 in 1977. No pozzolan or
supplementary cementitious material was specified in the original mix to mitigate potential ASR. ASR was not reported in the 1995 or 2005 inspections and was first noted (as 'possible map cracking') in the
2012 Part 12D inspection. It was confirmed as ASR by the 2017 inspection team based on the characteristic
cracking pattern and gel exudation. The reaction has become visually more prominent between 2017 and 2022,
with the affected area expanding from approximately 3,000 square feet to 5,000 square feet on the downstream
face. The combination of ASR (which creates microcracking throughout the concrete matrix) and freeze-thaw
cycling (which exploits those microcracks by ice crystal growth) is a well-documented synergistic deterioration
mechanism that accelerates both processes beyond what either would cause individually. Recommendation: Concrete coring from the gallery through the dam section is needed to quantify the depth
and severity of both deterioration mechanisms. Testing should include compressive and splitting tensile
strength at multiple depths, petrographic analysis per ASTM C856, and residual expansion testing per ASTM
C1293 to assess whether the ASR has potential for continued expansion. CDSC Project No.

Cascade Dam Safety Consultants Part 12D Inspection — Juniper Canyon Dam
3.3 Issue 3 — Left Abutment Seepage Increase (MODERATE Priority)
Left abutment seepage has increased from 8 gpm at first filling (1964) to 28 gpm at the time of this inspection
(2022). This represents a 250 percent increase over 58 years, with the rate of increase accelerating in the last
decade. Between 2000 and 2010, the seepage increased by approximately 5 gpm; between 2010 and 2022, it
increased by 8 gpm — nearly double the previous decade's rate. The seepage remains clear at all measurement points, with no turbidity, discoloration, or suspended material. This is an important finding: clear seepage indicates that the water is flowing through the rock mass and grout
curtain remnants without transporting material, meaning internal erosion has not initiated along the seepage
pathway. However, the increasing flow rate confirms that the seepage conduit is becoming more transmissive
over time, most likely due to progressive dissolution of the grout curtain in the shear zone area. The seepage path is believed to be along the shear zone that crosses the foundation beneath the left portion of
the gravity section and continues into the left abutment embankment foundation. The original grout curtain
treated this zone with 3,200 sacks of cement (18 percent of the total grout consumption), reducing the zone
permeability from 35 Lugeon to 3 Lugeon. The grout appears to have deteriorated over 59 years, allowing
progressively more seepage. The correlation between declining drain efficiency (Issue 1) and increasing left
abutment seepage is significant: as the drains become less effective at intercepting seepage below the gravity
section, more water bypasses the drainage system and exits at the left abutment via the shear zone. Consequence: The increasing seepage raises pore pressures in the left embankment foundation, which
reduces the embankment slope stability factor of safety. While the seepage is currently clear (no erosion), the
trend is adverse and the accelerating rate warrants investigation.

title: PART 12D SAFETY INSPECTION REPORT
content:
While the seepage is currently clear (no erosion), the
trend is adverse and the accelerating rate warrants investigation. If the grout curtain continues to deteriorate
and seepage reaches 50 gpm or more, the pore pressure increase could reduce the left embankment stability
below FHSC minimum criteria. The right abutment seepage has remained essentially stable at 7 gpm since
1964, confirming that the issue is specific to the left abutment (shear zone) pathway. 3.4 Issue 4 — Spillway Gate 2 Corrosion (MODERATE Priority)
Spillway radial Gate 2 (center gate, 30 ft wide × 22 ft high) continues to exhibit progressive corrosion that was
first documented in the 1995 dam safety inspection as 'visible surface corrosion on downstream skin plate.'
Over the past 27 years, the corrosion has progressed from surface coating failure to measurable metal section
loss. The condition of Gate 2 contrasts with Gates 1 and 3, which are in fair condition with localized coating
deterioration but no significant section loss. Specific findings for Gate 2: (1) The original 3-coat alkyd paint system has failed on approximately 90 percent of
the downstream skin plate surface, with heavy rust and pitting visible. (2) Ultrasonic thickness (UT)
measurements performed during the 2018 annual inspection documented section loss of up to 15 percent of the
original 3/8-inch skin plate thickness (0.375 inches original, 0.319 inches minimum measured). (3) The trunnion
bearings show excessive play (0.08 inches, measured during the 2020 annual inspection), exceeding the
0.05-inch limit for radial gates of this size per USACE EM 1110-2-2702. The bearings require frequent greasing
(monthly versus the normal quarterly schedule). (4) The downstream side seal is leaking approximately 2 gpm
at normal pool. (5) The hydraulic operating cylinder functions but is slow to initiate movement, suggesting
internal seal degradation. Consequence: Gate 2 is not currently structurally compromised (the 15 percent section loss is below the 20
percent threshold for structural concern), but the deterioration rate is accelerating and the trunnion bearing
condition raises concerns about gate operability during a flood event.

1.0 INTRODUCTION
Intermountain Dam Safety Engineers, LLC (IDSE) was retained by Juniper Basin Irrigation District (JBID) to
perform a geotechnical and concrete investigation of the gravity section as part of the Periodic Safety Review
(PSR) recommended by the 2022 FHSC Part 12D Safety Inspection (CDSC, October 2022). The 2022
inspection identified five issues requiring investigation; this report addresses the three issues that directly affect
the gravity section: (1) foundation drain deterioration and increasing uplift pressure, (2) concrete deterioration
from alkali-silica reaction (ASR) and freeze-thaw damage, and (3) seismic re-evaluation under the updated
NGSI 2018 hazard. The investigation comprised three exploratory borings through and adjacent to the gravity section, extensive
laboratory testing on concrete cores and foundation rock specimens, and engineering analysis of sliding
stability under current and remediated conditions. This report presents the field investigation, laboratory results,
and stability analysis for the gravity section. Companion reports address the embankment investigation (IDSE,
2025b), seepage and uplift analysis (IDSE, 2025c), and remediation design recommendations (IDSE, 2025d). 2.0 FIELD INVESTIGATION
Three exploratory borings (BH-GS-01, BH-GS-02, and BH-GS-03) were drilled in the gravity section between
August 4 and August 15, 2025.

2.1 BH-GS-01 — Gallery Boring (Concrete + Foundation)
BH-GS-01 was drilled from the drainage gallery floor (El. 5032.0) vertically through the gravity dam base and
into the foundation rock to a total depth of 85 feet. This is the most important boring in the investigation program
because it provides a complete vertical profile through both the concrete section and the underlying foundation,
including the shear zone. The upper 28 feet penetrated mass concrete (the dam base above the gallery), and
the remaining 57 feet penetrated foundation rock of varying lithology. Core recovery was 98 percent in concrete
and 95 percent in rock, with recovery losses concentrated in the shear zone (48-52 ft depth) where the clay
gouge was difficult to retain in the core barrel. The foundation rock sequence encountered in BH-GS-01 is consistent with the stratigraphy documented in the
original 1959 design borings (BH-3 and BH-4), confirming that the geological model established during design

3.2 Petrographic Analysis (ASTM C856)
Petrographic examination was performed on six thin sections prepared from concrete cores at depths of 1-2,
3-4, 6-7, 10-11, 16-17, and 24-25 feet. The examination was conducted by Intermountain Materials Testing
Laboratory (Boise, Idaho) following ASTM C856 Standard Practice for Petrographic Examination of Hardened
Concrete. The reactive constituent was positively identified as devitrified volcanic glass and strained quartz within the
rhyolite tuff coarse aggregate particles. In the original volcanic rock, the glass was in an amorphous,
high-energy state; over geologic time it partially crystallized (devitrified) to microcrystalline cristobalite and
tridymite — both metastable forms of silica that are susceptible to attack by the alkali hydroxides in the cement
pore solution. The reaction produces an amorphous alkali-silica gel (sodium-potassium-calcium silicate hydrate)
that absorbs water and expands, generating internal tensile stresses that cause the characteristic map cracking
observed on exposed surfaces.

The petrographic results define three distinct zones: (1) Active ASR (0 to 6 feet) — gel present in cracks and
voids, reaction rims on all coarse aggregate particles, connected microcracking network, expansion ongoing. (2) Incipient ASR (6 to 10 feet) — reaction rims forming on aggregate particles but no gel production yet; this
zone will eventually develop active ASR as moisture penetrates deeper. (3) Sound concrete (below 12 feet) —
no ASR indicators of any kind; the interior is fully protected by the sheer mass of concrete which limits moisture
diffusion to the surface zones. Carbonation depth was measured at 1.2 inches from the exposed gallery surface, which is within the normal
range for 62-year-old mass concrete in a saturated environment. The carbonation front has not reached the
reinforcement (the gallery lining has minimal reinforcing steel, and the gravity section itself is unreinforced mass
concrete), so carbonation-induced corrosion is not a concern. 4.0 FOUNDATION ROCK PROPERTIES

the first comprehensive characterization of the foundation since the original 1959 design investigation.

4.0 FOUNDATION ROCK PROPERTIES
Laboratory testing of the foundation rock specimens recovered from all three gravity section borings provides
the first comprehensive characterization of the foundation since the original 1959 design investigation. The
2025 testing program includes unconfined compressive strength (ASTM D7012 Method C) with deformation
measurement (elastic modulus and Poisson's ratio), indirect tensile strength (ASTM D3967), and residual shear
strength of the shear zone clay gouge (ring shear, ASTM D6467). IDSE Project No. 2025-DSE-0041 Page 5

4.1 Densely Welded Rhyolite Tuff
Eight UCS specimens were tested from the densely welded tuff zones in BH-GS-01, BH-GS-02, and BH-LE-01
(the left embankment boring also penetrated the same tuff formation below the embankment). The densely
welded tuff is a strong, brittle rock with a mean UCS of 15,180 psi (standard deviation 1,650 psi) and a range of
12,200 to 17,800 psi. The elastic modulus (E50, measured at 50 percent of peak stress) averages 5,820 ksi
with a range of 4,800 to 6,900 ksi. Poisson's ratio averages 0.20 (range 0.18 to 0.23). The indirect tensile strength (ITS, Brazilian test) was measured on 10 specimens, yielding a mean of 978 psi
with a range of 820 to 1,150 psi. The UCS-to-ITS ratio is 15.5, which is within the typical range of 10 to 20 for
volcanic rocks and indicates moderately brittle behavior. The unit weight of 152 pcf reflects the partially vitreous
(glassy) matrix of the welded tuff, which has lower density than crystalline igneous rocks like granite (typically
165 pcf). All specimens failed in brittle shear — a clean fracture surface inclined at 25 to 30 degrees to the loading axis,
with no plastic deformation visible on the stress-strain curves. The crack initiation (CI) threshold averaged 42
percent of peak stress, and the crack damage (CD) threshold averaged 78 percent of peak stress. The
post-peak residual strength averaged 18 percent of peak, confirming the brittle character of this rock type. These stress-strain characteristics are important for understanding the dam foundation behavior under seismic
loading — the rock will fail suddenly rather than deforming plastically. IDSE Project No. 2025-DSE-0041 Page 6

Intermountain Dam Safety Engineers, LLC Geotech & Concrete Investigation — Gravity Section
4.2 Olivine Basalt Interbed
Five UCS specimens were tested from the basalt interbeds in BH-GS-02 and BH-GS-03.

title: GEOTECHNICAL AND CONCRETE INVESTIGATION
content:
The basalt is
significantly stronger than the welded tuff, with a mean UCS of 30,480 psi (standard deviation 2,400 psi),
approximately double the tuff strength. The elastic modulus averages 10,180 ksi (range 8,800 to 11,500 ksi),
and Poisson's ratio averages 0.17. The unit weight of 172 pcf is typical for dense olivine basalt. Ten ITS specimens from the basalt yielded a mean tensile strength of 2,045 psi (range 1,750 to 2,350 psi). The
UCS-to-ITS ratio of 14.9 is comparable to the welded tuff, indicating similar brittleness despite the much higher
absolute strength. The basalt interbeds are excellent foundation rock where encountered, but they are
discontinuous — present as individual flow units 5 to 17 feet thick interbedded with the tuff. The permeability
contrast at basalt flow contacts (vesicular zones with high secondary porosity) creates preferential seepage
pathways that were treated by the original grout curtain. 4.3 Partially Welded Tuff
The partially welded tuff zones are significantly weaker than the densely welded material, with UCS ranging
from 1,500 to 3,800 psi (mean 2,650 psi) and RQD of only 15 to 35 percent. These zones represent the
gradational transition from densely welded (hot, compacted) to non-welded (cooler, uncompacted) portions of
the original ignimbrite cooling unit. The high porosity and low strength make these zones susceptible to
weathering and seepage, but they occur as relatively thin (2 to 5 feet) horizons bounded by competent densely
welded tuff and do not form continuous weak planes in the foundation.

5.0 SHEAR ZONE CHARACTERIZATION
The shear zone was encountered at 48 to 52 feet depth in BH-GS-01 and at 35 to 38 feet depth in BH-GS-02. These depths are geometrically consistent with a planar feature dipping 35 degrees to the southeast, matching
the geometry established by BH-3 and BH-4 in the 1959 investigation. The zone width is 2-4 feet in BH-GS-01,
identical to the 1959 measurement in BH-3, indicating that the shear zone has not widened or been altered by
62 years of seepage. IDSE Project No. 2025-DSE-0041 Page 7

The central gouge seam was sampled by Shelby tube in BH-GS-01. The gouge is a high-plasticity clay (USCS
classification CH) with a liquid limit of 52, plasticity index of 28, and a clay fraction of 62 percent. The clay
mineralogy is dominated by montmorillonite (smectite group), which is consistent with the high plasticity and is
the product of hydrothermal alteration of the volcanic rock along the shear plane. The gouge surfaces are
prominently slickensided in at least two directions, indicating repeated shear displacement — this is a
geologically mature fault gouge that has been sheared well beyond its peak strength. Residual shear strength was measured by ring shear testing (ASTM D6467) on reconstituted gouge samples at
normal stresses of 500, 1,000, 2,000, and 4,000 psf. The residual strength parameters are c'r = 50 psf and f'r =
12°. The very low residual friction angle of 12° is consistent with the high clay fraction and montmorillonite
content — montmorillonite clays typically exhibit residual friction angles of 8° to 15° depending on the
percentage of clay-size particles. For comparison, direct shear testing on intact gouge specimens yielded peak
strength parameters of c' = 180 psf and f' = 18°; however, the residual parameters are used for design because
the slickensided surfaces indicate that the peak strength has already been exceeded by tectonic shearing. The shear zone permeability was measured at 5e-05 cm/s by falling-head testing on the gouge material, which
is three orders of magnitude higher than the surrounding intact welded tuff (~10nn cm/s for the rock matrix). This confirms that the shear zone is a preferential seepage conduit through the foundation, as evidenced by the
concentration of drain flows at Drains 18 through 22 (directly above the shear zone) and the left abutment
seepage that follows the zone beneath the embankment foundation.

6.0 GRAVITY SECTION STABILITY ANALYSIS
Sliding stability of the concrete gravity section was evaluated per FHSC Engineering Guidelines Chapter 3
using the gravity method (rigid body equilibrium) for the maximum height cross-section (Monolith 8, height =
185 ft, base width = 148 ft). Uplift pressures were based on the measured piezometric data from the gallery
floor piezometers, not assumed triangular or bilinear distributions. The analysis used the unbonded
concrete-to-rock interface friction angle of 38° (conservative; bonded assumption is 45°) with zero cohesion. Seven load cases were analyzed, spanning the range of drain conditions from current (52 percent efficiency) to
fully failed (0 percent) to rehabilitated (80+ percent), under normal pool, PMF, and MCE (0.18g) loading. The
results demonstrate that drain condition is the dominant variable controlling gravity section stability. Table 6-1: Gravity Section Sliding Stability Results — Monolith 8

content:
The margin
is only 1.3 percent — any further deterioration of drain efficiency will cause the factor of safety to fall below the
minimum. If the drains fail completely (efficiency drops to zero, uplift rises to an estimated 67 percent of headwater), the
normal pool FS drops to 1.18 — well below the 1.50 minimum and approaching the threshold for potential
sliding failure. The PMF and MCE cases are already inadequate under current conditions (FS 1.28 and 1.05
respectively, both below their minimum criteria). With drain rehabilitation restoring efficiency to 80 percent or better (reducing uplift to approximately 30 percent
of headwater), all seven load cases meet FHSC minimum criteria. The normal pool FS improves from 1.52 to
2.15 — a 41 percent improvement — solely from reducing uplift. The MCE case improves from 1.05 to 1.38,
meeting the 1.10 minimum. This demonstrates that drain rehabilitation is the single most effective remedial
measure for the gravity section. 7.0 CONCLUSIONS AND RECOMMENDATIONS
1. Foundation drain rehabilitation is the single most critical remedial action for the gravity section. Restoring drain efficiency from the current 52 percent to the design target of 80 percent or better would reduce
uplift from 48 percent to approximately 30 percent of headwater, increasing the normal pool sliding factor of
safety from 1.52 to 2.15. IDSE recommends a combined rehabilitation approach: mechanical and chemical
cleaning of the existing 42 drains, supplemented by 10 new drains at 5-foot spacing in the shear zone area
(Drains 16-26 zone) where clogging is most severe. See the Foundation Drain Evaluation report (IDSE, 2025e)
for detailed rehabilitation alternatives. IDSE Project No. 2025-DSE-0041 Page 9

2. Concrete deterioration is significant but not yet structural. The outer 4 to 6 feet of the upstream face is
severely degraded by the combined effects of ASR and freeze-thaw cycling, with compressive strength reduced
to 3,420 psi (a 43 percent reduction from the sound interior). However, 75 to 80 percent of the cross-section
retains full structural capacity. The interior concrete has gained strength to 6,050 psi — 17 percent above the
original 28-day mean of 5,180 psi. IDSE recommends a 4-inch fiber-reinforced shotcrete overlay on the
upstream face (El. 5,160 to 5,185, approximately 5,400 square feet) to arrest further deterioration. See the
Concrete Condition Assessment (IDSE, 2025f) for repair alternatives. 3. Seismic adequacy requires drain rehabilitation first. The MCE factor of safety under current conditions
(1.05) is inadequate, but with drains rehabilitated it improves to 1.38, meeting the FHSC minimum of 1.10. If
drain rehabilitation alone does not achieve the target uplift reduction, supplemental post-tensioned rock anchors
may be required; however, IDSE expects that drain rehabilitation will be sufficient based on the 1964 baseline
performance (85 percent efficiency, uplift only 28 percent of headwater). 4. The foundation rock is competent and has not degraded. The 2025 rock testing results are consistent
with the 1959 design-phase characterization. The densely welded tuff (mean UCS 15,180 psi, RQD 82%) and
basalt interbed (mean UCS 30,480 psi) provide an excellent foundation for the gravity section. The weak link in
the foundation is the shear zone clay gouge (residual f'r = 12°), which controls the seepage pathway and
influences the uplift distribution but does not form a through-going sliding surface at the dam base. IDSE Project No. 2025-DSE-0041 Page 10

2.2 BH-GS-02 — Downstream Toe (Foundation Only)
BH-GS-02 was drilled at the downstream toe of the gravity section (El. 5,020.5) to a total depth of 75 feet,
penetrating foundation rock only (no concrete). This boring was positioned to characterize the foundation
downstream of the grout curtain and to intersect the shear zone at a shallower depth than BH-GS-01, providing
a second data point for the shear zone geometry. The shear zone was encountered at 35 to 38 feet depth,
which is consistent with the 35° dip projected from the 48 to 52 foot depth in BH-GS-01 — confirming the
continuous, planar geometry of this feature across the dam foundation. A vibrating-wire (VW) piezometer was installed at 55 feet depth (below the shear zone and downstream of the
grout curtain) to provide a continuous record of foundation pore pressure at a location not monitored by the
existing gallery instruments. The initial reading at installation indicated a pore pressure head of 38 feet, which is
consistent with the elevated uplift measured by the gallery piezometers and confirms that the grout curtain is
not fully effective at preventing seepage into the downstream foundation rock. The rock quality in BH-GS-02 is comparable to BH-GS-01 — densely welded tuff with RQD of 78 to 82 percent
above and below the shear zone, and a thick basalt interbed from 55 to 70 feet with RQD of 90 percent. The
vesicular flow contact at 55 feet was noted as a permeable feature (visible water inflow during drilling),
consistent with the high Lugeon values measured at basalt contacts in the 1959 design borings. 2.3 BH-GS-03 — Right Monolith / Spillway Area
BH-GS-03 was drilled at the right gravity monolith adjacent to the spillway structure (Sta. 10+40, El. 5,025.0) to
a total depth of 50 feet. The purpose was to characterize the basalt interbed, which is thicker and more
prominent on the right side of the canyon.

The strength gradient is dramatic. The outer 4 feet of concrete — the zone exposed to both moisture (from
gallery surfaces, construction joints, and direct reservoir contact) and freeze-thaw cycling — has lost 43 percent
of its compressive strength and 51 percent of its tensile strength relative to the sound interior concrete. The
compressive strength at 0 to 4 feet (3,420 psi) has fallen below the original 28-day design minimum of 4,500 psi
by 24 percent. In contrast, the interior concrete (below 14 feet from exposed surfaces) has actually gained strength over the
62-year service life. The measured compressive strength at 20 to 28 feet depth is 6,050 psi, exceeding the
original 28-day mean of 5,180 psi by 17 percent. This continued strength gain is expected in mass concrete
with Type II cement, where long-term hydration of residual unhydrated cement particles increases strength for
decades after placement. The tensile strength of the interior concrete (500 psi) is also well above the typical
range for mass concrete. Critical conclusion: Approximately 75 to 80 percent of the gravity section cross-section (the interior, more than
8 to 10 feet from any exposed surface) retains full structural capacity. The deterioration is a surface
phenomenon advancing inward. The rate of advance is estimated at 0.5 to 1.0 inches per decade based on
comparison of the 1995 inspection findings (0.25-inch scaling) with the current damage front (3 to 4 inches). At
this rate, the damage would require another 50 to 100 years to penetrate to the structural core of the dam. However, repair is recommended now to arrest the progression and protect the long-term durability of the
upstream face. IDSE Project No. 2025-DSE-0041 Page 4

Intermountain Dam Safety Engineers, LLC Geotech Investigation — Embankments
1.0 INTRODUCTION
Intermountain Dam Safety Engineers, LLC (IDSE) performed a geotechnical investigation of the left and right
embankment abutment transitions as part of the Periodic Safety Review (PSR) of Juniper Canyon Dam. The
investigation was driven by two concerns identified in the 2022 FHSC Part 12D inspection: (1) increasing left
abutment seepage (from 8 gpm at first filling in 1964 to 35 gpm in 2025), and (2) the need to re-evaluate
embankment stability under the updated seismic hazard (0.18g PGA, an 80 percent increase over the original
design value of 0.10g). The investigation comprised two exploratory borings — one through each embankment — with continuous
sampling, in-situ testing, laboratory characterization of embankment fill materials and foundation rock, and
slope stability analysis under static, seismic, and rapid drawdown conditions. This report presents the field and
laboratory results and the stability evaluation for both embankments. The left embankment is the focus because
it overlies the shear zone that is the primary seepage conduit through the foundation (see the Geotechnical and
Concrete Investigation — Gravity Section, IDSE 2025a, for the shear zone characterization). The right
embankment serves as a control case with stable seepage history.

title: GEOTECHNICAL INVESTIGATION REPORT
content:
The right
embankment serves as a control case with stable seepage history. Both embankments are zoned earthfill structures with a compacted silty clay core (Zone 1, CL-ML), processed
sand filter (Zone 2, SP-SM), and compacted tuff rockfill shells (Zone 3, GW-GM). The left embankment is 140
feet long with a maximum height of 65 feet; the right embankment is 140 feet long with a maximum height of 55
feet. Both are founded on densely welded rhyolite tuff, with dental concrete at the foundation contact and the
grout curtain extending through the foundation beneath each embankment. 2.0 FIELD INVESTIGATION

3.2 Gradation and Classification
Four gradation analyses with hydrometer (ASTM D422/D7928) were performed on core zone samples from
both embankments. The material is broadly graded: approximately 6 to 8 percent gravel, 30 to 38 percent sand,
31 to 37 percent silt, and 24 to 30 percent clay (mean 27 percent clay by hydrometer). The clay fraction is
primarily illite with minor kaolinite — non-expansive clay minerals consistent with the weathered volcanic tuff

the 4.0 limit for cohesive base soils. The filter is performing its intended function of preventing migration of core
fines into the shell while allowing drainage.

With the recommended remediation (supplemental grouting of the shear zone beneath the left abutment plus
drain rehabilitation), the left embankment meets all FHSC stability criteria. The static FS improves from 1.38 to
1.15 (a -17 percent improvement), the seismic FS improves from 1.62 to 1.22, and the rapid drawdown FS

condition and the stability deficiency is caused solely by the foundation seepage condition. IDSE Project No. 2025-DSE-0041 Page 8

2.2 Core Zone Moisture Conditions
The core zone (Zone 1) moisture content profile provides important information about the current state of the
embankment. Above the phreatic surface (0 to 38 feet depth), the moisture content ranges from 17.5 to 19.0
percent — close to the optimum moisture content (OMC) of 17.5 percent, indicating that the fill above the water
table has maintained approximately its as-placed condition after 62 years. Below 38 feet, the core zone is fully
saturated, with moisture contents of 19.5 to 22.0 percent — 2 to 5 percentage points above OMC. The phreatic surface elevation (approximately El. 5,164, corresponding to 38 feet below the crest at El. 5,202)
is consistent with the downstream piezometer readings and indicates that the core zone is functioning as an
effective seepage barrier. If the core were compromised (cracked, eroded, or internally eroded), the phreatic
surface would be higher and the moisture contents above 38 feet would be elevated. The fact that the phreatic
surface is at its expected position confirms that the left abutment seepage increase is through the foundation
(shear zone), not through the embankment fill. 2.3 BH-RE-01 — Right Embankment (Control)
BH-RE-01 was drilled from the right embankment crest (Sta. 14+80, El. 5202.0) to a total depth of 60 feet. The
subsurface profile is similar to the left embankment: crest road fill, rockfill shell, sand filter, silty clay core
(CL-ML), dental concrete at the foundation contact, and competent welded tuff below. The critical difference from BH-LE-01 is the behavior in the foundation rock. No elevated water levels or
increased water inflow were encountered during drilling at any depth in BH-RE-01. The welded tuff foundation
beneath the right embankment is competent (RQD 82 percent) with tight joints and no evidence of the shear
zone.

title: GEOTECHNICAL INVESTIGATION REPORT
content:
The welded tuff foundation
beneath the right embankment is competent (RQD 82 percent) with tight joints and no evidence of the shear
zone. This is consistent with the geological model: the shear zone, dipping at 35 degrees to the southeast,
passes beneath the gravity section and the left abutment but does not extend to the right abutment. The right abutment seepage has remained essentially constant at 7 gpm since first filling in 1964 — unchanged
over 61 years. This stable seepage history, combined with the absence of any transmissive features in the
foundation boring, confirms that the right embankment and its foundation are performing as designed. A VW
piezometer was installed at 50 feet depth in BH-RE-01 to provide a baseline for long-term monitoring, but no
inclinometer was installed. 3.0 EMBANKMENT FILL PROPERTIES

Intermountain Dam Safety Engineers, LLC Instrumentation Summary — Juniper Canyon Dam
1.0 INTRODUCTION
This report summarizes the instrumentation monitoring data for Juniper Canyon Dam from 2005 to 2025, with
reference to baseline readings established during first filling (1964) and key historical benchmarks. The dam's
instrumentation system was installed during construction (1960-1963) and has been read on regular schedules
since first filling in October 1963. Two new instruments were added during the 2025 PSR investigation: a
vibrating-wire (VW) piezometer in the left embankment foundation (BH-LE-01, 65 ft depth) and an inclinometer
casing in the same boring (to 75 ft depth). A second VW piezometer was installed at BH-GS-02 (55 ft depth,
downstream of the grout curtain). The 20-year period from 2005 to 2025 is of particular interest because it spans the transition from marginal

1. Drain efficiency is the master variable. The 20-year record demonstrates that drain efficiency decline
drives every other adverse trend: rising uplift (R-squared = 0.97 correlation), increasing left abutment seepage
(R-squared = 0.94), rising left embankment foundation pore pressures (R-squared = 0.91), and increasing

monitoring period: seepage (7 gpm, unchanged since 1964), piezometers (stable), structural measurements
(stable). The right abutment has no shear zone, no grout curtain deterioration, and no adverse trends. This
demonstrates that the adverse trends on the left side are caused by the site-specific geological condition (shear
zone + deteriorated grout curtain), not by general aging of the dam. 3. Structural measurements are stable. Despite the elevated uplift, the gravity section structural response

1.0 INTRODUCTION

dam. This evaluation documents the current condition of all 42 drains based on visual inspection, downhole
video survey, individual flow measurement, and chemical analysis of the clogging deposits. The evaluation was
performed between September 8 and September 12, 2025. 2.0 DRAIN INVENTORY AND CONDITION ASSESSMENT

standpipe, and weir at the gallery floor; (2) flow measurement — individual drain flow measured at the V-notch
weir under normal pool conditions (El. 5195.0); (3) downhole video — miniature camera (Aries Industries,
0.75-inch diameter) inserted to full depth or to the obstruction; and (4) deposit sampling — samples of clogging

Intermountain Dam Safety Engineers, LLC Foundation Drain Evaluation — Juniper Canyon Dam
2.1 Downhole Video Findings
The video survey revealed three distinct deposit morphologies: (1) Collar blockage — thick, hard calcium
carbonate (calcite) deposits within the first 1 to 8 feet of the drain collar, formed by CO2 degassing as seepage
water enters the low-pressure gallery environment. This is the primary clogging mechanism and accounts for
the complete blockage at all 8 fully clogged drains. The deposits are concentrically layered, white to cream
colored, and extremely hard — a geologist's hammer was required to break samples for analysis. (2) Bore wall coating — a thin (1 to 5 mm) calcite film lining the entire bore wall from collar to total depth on all
partially clogged and functional drains. This coating progressively reduces the bore diameter and the hydraulic
conductivity of the drain. At the current coating thickness, the bore diameter is reduced from the original 3
inches to approximately 2.0 to 2.5 inches in most drains, reducing the hydraulic capacity by 30 to 50 percent
even where the drain is not completely blocked. (3) Shear zone intersection deposits — in Drains 16 through 26 (the shear zone area), the video showed
iron-stained, rust-orange deposits at the intersection of the drain bore with the shear zone (approximately 20 to
25 feet below the gallery floor). These deposits are mixed iron hydroxide and calcite, formed by oxidation of
dissolved iron from the clay gouge. They are softer than the collar deposits and may be removable by chemical
treatment alone.

The 2025 Periodic Safety Review of Juniper Canyon Dam has identified five deficiencies requiring remediation. This report presents the recommended remediation program, organized into three phases over three

(FS = 1.38 versus 1.50 required) due to elevated foundation pore pressures along the shear zone. The good
news is that both deficiencies are correctable by restoring the drain and grouting systems. 2.0 SUMMARY OF DEFICIENCIES

title: REMEDIATION DESIGN RECOMMENDATIONS
content:
Intermountain Dam Safety Engineers, LLC Remediation — Juniper Canyon Dam
3.0 PHASE 1 — CRITICAL REMEDIATION (2026)
3.1 Foundation Drain Rehabilitation
The recommended approach combines mechanical and chemical cleaning of all 42 existing drains with 10 new
supplemental drains in the shear zone area. The existing drains will be cleaned by high-pressure water jetting
(6,000 psi) followed by hydrochloric acid treatment (10 percent HCl solution, 4-hour soak time) to dissolve the
calcium carbonate deposits. Each drain will be re-reamed to full diameter with a mechanical bit, then
video-inspected to verify that the bore is clear to full depth (40 feet). Drains that cannot be rehabilitated by this
method will be re-drilled on a 2-foot offset. The 10 supplemental drains will be drilled at 5-foot spacing between the existing drains in the shear zone area
(Drains 16 through 26 zone, approximately Sta. 7+60 to Sta. 8+60 in the gallery). This is the zone where
clogging is most severe (8 of the 8 fully clogged drains are in this zone) because the shear zone delivers the
highest mineral-laden seepage to the drain bore. The supplemental drains will be 3-inch diameter NX holes
drilled to 50 feet depth (10 feet deeper than the existing drains) to improve interception of the shear zone
seepage. Expected outcome: Drain efficiency restored to 80-85 percent, uplift reduced from 48 percent to approximately
30 percent of headwater, gravity section normal pool FS improved from 1.52 to 2.15. Estimated cost: $280K
to $380K. Duration: 4-6 weeks. 3.2 Left Abutment Supplemental Grouting
A single-line supplemental grout curtain will be constructed along 120 feet of the left abutment foundation (Sta. 4+00 to 5+20), centered on the shear zone intersection with the embankment foundation. Grout holes will be
drilled at 5-foot primary spacing from the left embankment crest and from the gallery, to a depth of 80 feet
(approximately 20 feet below the shear zone at this location). Split-spacing to 2.5 feet will be performed where
refusal pressures exceed 5 Lugeon at the primary spacing.

title: REMEDIATION DESIGN RECOMMENDATIONS
content:
Split-spacing to 2.5 feet will be performed where
refusal pressures exceed 5 Lugeon at the primary spacing. Microfine cement grout (Blaine fineness > 800 m2/kg, maximum particle size 15 microns) is recommended for
the shear zone interval (65 to 75 feet depth) to achieve better penetration into the fine fractures and clay gouge
that conventional Portland cement grout cannot enter. Standard Type I Portland cement grout (water-cement
ratios from 5:1 to 0.6:1, per the standard split-spacing and thickening protocol) will be used above and below
the shear zone interval. Estimated total grout consumption is 800 to 1,200 sacks (94 lb each). Grouting
pressures will be limited to 0.5 psi per foot of depth to prevent hydraulic fracturing. Expected outcome: Left abutment seepage reduced from 35 gpm to approximately 12 gpm. Left embankment
static FS improved from 1.38 to 1.15. Foundation pore pressure at VW-LE01 (the new vibrating-wire piezometer
at 65 feet depth in BH-LE-01) reduced by approximately 50 percent. Estimated cost: $220K to $320K. Duration: 3-4 weeks. 3.3 Enhanced Monitoring System
An automated data acquisition system will be installed to provide continuous real-time monitoring of the two
new VW piezometers (VW-GS02 and VW-LE01) and a new automated rain gauge. The system will include a
Campbell Scientific CR6 datalogger, cellular modem for remote data transmission, solar panel and battery for
power, and web-based data visualization platform accessible by JBID operations staff and IDSE engineers. Alert thresholds will be programmed to trigger email/SMS notifications when pore pressures exceed defined
limits (see Emergency Action Plan Update, JBID 2025). IDSE Project No. 2025-DSE-0041 Page 2

Intermountain Dam Safety Engineers, LLC Remediation — Juniper Canyon Dam
4.0 PHASE 2 — HIGH PRIORITY REPAIRS (2027)
4.1 Upstream Face Repair
A 4-inch fiber-reinforced shotcrete overlay is recommended for the upstream face of the gravity section within
the freeze-thaw damage zone (El. 5,160 to El. 5,185, approximately 5,400 square feet). The shotcrete will be
wet-mix, applied by robotic nozzle from a suspended platform, with a non-reactive basalt coarse aggregate
(imported, verified per ASTM C1260), Type V cement with 20 percent Class F fly ash, w/c ratio of 0.42
maximum, air content of 6 plus or minus 1.5 percent, and macro synthetic fiber reinforcement at 6 lb/cy. This
mix eliminates all three deficiencies of the original concrete: reactive aggregate, high-alkali cement, and
absence of pozzolan. The design life of the overlay is 30 to 40 years. Surface preparation: the deteriorated concrete (scaling and spalling to 3-4 inch depth) will be removed by
hydrodemolition (20,000 psi water jet) to expose sound concrete with a roughened, irregular surface for
shotcrete bond. The hydrodemolition removes only weak material and creates a superior bonding surface
compared to mechanical chipping. A silane sealer will be applied to the downstream face ASR cracks to reduce
moisture penetration and slow the reaction rate. The silane is a penetrating sealer that does not form a surface
film — it allows the concrete to breathe while reducing water absorption by 80 to 90 percent. Estimated cost: $180K to $260K. Duration: 4-6 weeks (September-October, during reservoir drawdown). 4.2 Spillway Gate 2 Rehabilitation
Gate 2 requires comprehensive rehabilitation: (1) Replace the downstream half of the skin plate (approximately
330 square feet of 3/8-inch A572 Grade 50 steel) where section loss exceeds 10 percent. The upstream half of
the skin plate retains adequate thickness and will be recoated. (2) Replace both trunnion bearings
(bronze-on-steel, manufacturer's specification).

title: REMEDIATION DESIGN RECOMMENDATIONS
content:
The upstream half of
the skin plate retains adequate thickness and will be recoated. (2) Replace both trunnion bearings
(bronze-on-steel, manufacturer's specification). (3) Full recoating with a 3-coat marine-grade epoxy system
(SSPC SP-10 surface preparation, zinc-rich primer, epoxy intermediate, and polyurethane topcoat). (4) Replace
J-seals and side seals. The work can be performed during the low-pool season (September-November) using
the existing bulkhead slots for gate isolation. Gates 1 and 3 should be spot-repaired and fully recoated on the same mobilization to prevent them from
reaching Gate 2's deteriorated condition. Estimated cost (all three gates): $350K to $480K. Duration: 6-8

improvements (such as post-tensioned rock anchors) would be required for the gravity section. Similarly, the left
embankment MCE FS would improve from 1.62 to 1.22, meeting criteria. If, however, the Phase 1 remediation does not fully achieve the target uplift reduction (e.g., if drain rehabilitation
